analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax entirely.
analysis.headline: The estate tax repeal bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the Senate Finance Committee until the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have permanently eliminated the federal taxes owed when large estates and gifts pass from one person to another. Only the largest estates — those above the tax-free threshold — ever owe estate tax, so the money saved would go almost entirely to the wealthiest families in the country. The bill never moved after being sent to the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates — families whose taxable wealth exceeds the exemption — would pay no federal estate tax, saving them up to 55% of the taxable amount at 1997 rates. Very wealthy families making large lifetime gifts or skipping generations would also benefit. The bill's sponsors argued the change would boost national savings and economic growth.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax for deaths and transfers after enactment, eliminating a top tax rate of up to 55% on large estates.
The bill's stated rationale is that estate taxes discourage savings and 'double tax' income, and that repeal would expand savings, investment, and entrepreneurship.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would forgo estate and gift tax revenue — in the mid-1990s roughly $15-20 billion per year — meaning other taxes would stay higher, services would be cut, or deficits would grow to make up the difference. Because only estates above the exemption threshold pay the tax, the revenue burden shifted would fall on everyone else through foregone public funds.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers generally, via lost revenue

drawbacks.text: Repeal eliminates a tax that in the 1990s applied only to estates above a several-hundred-thousand-dollar exemption, so its benefits concentrate entirely among the wealthiest families while the lost revenue is borne broadly.

The repeal would take effect immediately upon enactment, with no phase-in, permanently removing a progressive source of federal revenue that exists largely because heirs did not earn the money themselves.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: large inheritances pass untaxed, which the sponsors argue would encourage savings and family businesses. The cost is broad: billions in annual federal revenue — collected almost exclusively from multi-million-dollar estates — disappears permanently, leaving the burden on other taxpayers or on public programs. For ordinary working people, the direct benefit is minimal and the fiscal cost is shared by all.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Lugar introduced the bill on January 21, 1997, with introductory remarks in the Senate.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — and the bill expired when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the estate tax remained in place, preserving a progressive revenue source paid almost entirely by the largest estates. Families with modest and mid-sized estates were unaffected either way, since they never owed the tax.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The estate tax stayed; no one else gained

for.name: Sen. Richard G. Lugar
for.role: U.S. Senator from Indiana, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the estate and gift tax repeal bill and delivered introductory remarks.

for.name: 6 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All seven supporters — the sponsor and six cosponsors — were Republicans, and no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored it; the record shows no roll-call votes either way.

industries.note: Full repeal would eliminate a tax of up to 55% on multi-million-dollar inheritances, a benefit flowing exclusively to families above the exemption threshold. The lost revenue would otherwise fund general federal spending borne by everyone.

industries.industry: Estate planning lawyers and wealth managers
industries.note: Full repeal would shrink demand for estate-tax planning, trusts, and life insurance products built around the tax. Consumers of those services would save planning costs.
